units.text: Use E C R when a build needs a managed registry, not a place to run the container. The pipeline builds and pushes an O C I image; the repository stores its manifest and layers, and the runtime later pulls that artifact.
A tag is a convenient name, while a digest identifies exact content. Record the deployed digest and decide independently who can pull, what gets scanned, what to retain, and where to replicate.

A failed image pull has three gates: caller permissions, repository access, and network reachability. For startup on E C S, check the task execution role rather than granting unrelated permissions to the application task role.

A token is not proof of access to every repository. Check the destination policy for cross-account pulls and reachability to the E C R interfaces and S three layers. Test from the actual runtime with the intended digest.

Before lifecycle cleanup, record the exact deployed digest and keep a known-good rollback digest, its multi-architecture manifests, and required artifacts. A movable tag alone cannot prove what will be redeployed.

Preview the lifecycle policy and verify that the deployment and rollback digests remain accessible before allowing expiry. If a tag must never point to new content, apply tag immutability; that is separate from retention.

Use E C R replication to distribute the image artifact, not to create a working application in another Region. Compare source and destination digests. In a cross-account destination, the registry policy must allow replication from the source.

Use explicit replication backfill for qualifying existing images when needed. At the destination, separately verify repository configuration, runtime access and the deployment. A replicated digest does not prove that a task is running.

Pick scanning coverage based on the packages you ship. Basic scanning covers supported operating-system vulnerabilities. Enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector and extends coverage to supported language packages; check the configured frequency.

Use the finding to decide what to remediate. Rebuild with patched dependencies, review the new digest and its scan results, then deploy the verified image. A past scan, or zero reported findings, is not proof of safety.

Amazon E K S runs the Kubernetes control plane. Your Pods run on the workload compute you select. This distinction matters because a healthy Kubernetes A P I does not tell you whether the application has enough healthy replicas.
Plan service exposure, workload identity, storage and upgrades separately. An E K S cluster is regional, so cross-Region recovery needs its own cluster and a data and traffic plan.

AWS manages E K S control-plane availability across Availability Zones. You still select workload compute and configure deployments, service access and workload identity. Treat these as separate availability responsibilities.

If one application Pod fails, the exam answer is not to add control-plane replicas. Check replica placement, health, runtime and storage. Use a separate regional recovery design when the requirement includes regional loss.

Choose compute by the operational responsibility you need. Managed node groups integrate node lifecycle, while self-managed nodes give you more control and leave you with more patching and upgrade work.

Fargate runs matching Pods without worker node administration, subject to platform constraints. E K S Auto Mode manages node compute and selected platform functions. Verify workload and add-on compatibility before selecting either.

A public application does not require public workers. The internet-facing load balancer accepts the request in public subnets and forwards it to allowed targets in private subnets. Choose the target type to match addressing.

Validate worker access to the Kubernetes A P I and the dependencies used for image pulls and logs. Health checks, controller permissions and security-group paths are separate checks. This is not a requirement to expose the Kubernetes A P I publicly.

Separate permissions to administer Kubernetes from permissions for a Pod to call AWS APIs. For cluster operations, configure cluster access and grant Kubernetes permissions as appropriate; the illustrated R B A C rules scope namespace and object actions.

For S three access from a Pod, associate its service account with a scoped I A M role using a supported workload identity option. E K S Pod Identity is not supported on Fargate; consider I R S A there rather than broadening the node role.

A persistent volume claim requests storage; the provisioner and topology determine whether the Pod can use it. E B S gives compatible Pods block storage in the same Availability Zone. It is not a shared regional filesystem and cannot be mounted by Fargate Pods.

Use E F S when supported workloads need a shared regional filesystem. For E K S Fargate, use static provisioning rather than assuming a dynamically provisioned E F S volume. Also check access mode and what should happen when the claim is deleted.

Choose the F S x integration by workload and driver, not by the F S x name alone. The example uses the Lustre C S I driver for a parallel filesystem, and NetApp Trident for eligible On Tap-backed storage. The F S x for Lustre C S I driver is not supported on Fargate.

Before choosing the storage class, verify the filesystem protocol, supported node placement, network access, I A M and reclaim behavior. Mount a test volume from a real Pod and check cleanup and recovery before relying on it.
